I'm not a libertarian and am not currently planning on becoming one, but I thought I would start a discussion on this topic because I feel that there are gaps in my understanding of the libertarian rationale behind the non-aggression principle. The main arguments for the non-aggression principle that I've heard are the consequentialist argument and the natural rights argument.

With the natural rights argument, it is stated that due to every individual's self-ownership, every individual owns the fruit of their labor. The argument continues by stating that it is therefore ethically wrong to initiate force against someone or the fruit of their labor because they rightfully own it. Libertarians use this to justify opposition to taxation, which they claim is theft of the fruit of one's labor. What is never justified in this argument is why this "theft by government" is ethically wrong. For example, if the government is taking from the rich and giving to the poor, it is insufficient to state that such an action would be inherently unethical because (according to this argument) it is theft.

tl;dr Even if you could demonstrate that taxation is theft, how would you then demonstrate that this "theft by government" is unethical?

With the consequentialist argument, some libertarians claim that even if the non-aggression principle is not an objective moral truth, adherence to it always leads to the best results. My question is: what evidence is there for this?

If you have other arguments besides these two for the non-aggression principle, I would be happy to read those also.
Help me understand the rationale behind the non-aggression principle

Basically if you think it is immoral, unjust, or illegal for an individual person to take a gun and go to a rich persons house to take their money by force and give it to a poor person, then how can it be just, moral, or legal for a group of people to do the same thing?

Basically if you think it is immoral, unjust, or illegal for an individual person to take a gun and go to a rich persons house to take their money by force and give it to a poor person, then how can it be just, moral, or legal for a group of people to do the same thing?

Whether or not I think being a "Robin Hood" is unethical isn't relevant. I'll try to answer your questions here.

What is never justified in this argument is why this "theft by government" is ethically wrong. For example, if the government is taking from the rich and giving to the poor, it is insufficient to state that such an action would be inherently unethical because (according to this argument) it is theft.

I, and many other libertarians, believe that such an action is ethically wrong because of what's known as the "moral hazard." The moral hazard is that if you use your resources to empower another, that person (or group) then becomes dependent on those resources, creating a situation where it is impossible to backpedal on such a promise without bringing harm to another.

Furthermore, we generally see such actions as immoral because it increases the power of the government at the expense of individual liberty. Example: the government has decreed that I must give a portion of my income to fund public education, and this gives me less liberty to use my income to make my own decisions on where my children will go to school.

We also typically see the government as an ineffectual institution to advance social welfare. The government has no incentive to do a good job, but it has strong incentives to expand programs which give it greater control over its subjects. A politician may campaign on a social welfare issue, but it's rare to see actual meaningful reform done in a professional manner.

A poignant example I'll use is the Affordable Care Act, which has numerous stipulations that make little sense. The ACA mandates that insurance companies can't spend more than 20% of their revenue on administrative costs, which was done in order to minimize "executive greed," but this stipulation was ignorant of the fact that companies that spent more than 20% of their revenue on administrative costs were usually the ones that were better at negotiating healthcare payment. Now insurance companies have an incentive to actually have higher healthcare costs.

This all culminates in the principle that I disagree with the notion that I should give up my resources to the government for a "good cause" because I see the government as a fundamentally flawed institution for such reform, and any action done as such is tyranny of the majority.

With the consequentialist argument, some libertarians claim that even if the non-aggression principle is not an objective moral truth, adherence to it always leads to the best results. My question is: what evidence is there for this?

Good question! Libertarianism is a political philosophy based on the principle of "egoism." Essentially egoism is the idea that I know myself best, and I am the one that has the most information at hand to make decisions regarding my own health and welfare. It is my natural interest to do what is in my own interest, and I can use my resources efficiently to achieve my goals. Conversely my neighbor knows less about me, and I know less about them. I am not qualified to make decisions on how much my neighbor should be paying in taxes, how much healthcare coverage they need, what food they should eat, who they should marry, etc., etc. The less my neighbor interferes in my life, the better it will be. The less I interfere in theirs, the better theirs will be.

Your request for evidence is sort of an inverted one. There's more evidence of the failure of government, but it's impossible to take a situation and say that it happened because the government did nothing. I would invite you to look at the success of countries that embrace liberty, but that's also a bit of a correlation/causation problem. Alexis de Tocqueville ruminated extensively on the industriousness that liberty fosters in people when they are in control of their own destiny though, and his thoughts are well known in his book Democracy in America.

Now you used the Robin Hood example of an "ethical" situation where it's okay for someone else to make a decision for another. If it's for a "good cause" it's okay, right? Well I personally (and I'm sure other libertarians as well) disagree with such sentiment because of what's known as the "road to serfdom." Without getting into the nitty gritty, the road to serfdom is essentially the idea that one cannot have political freedom without economic freedom. When the state has power over your means, you are beholden to the state and lose your liberty. The book, written by Hayek, is actually based on Nazi Germany, but is certainly applicable to other fascist and communist regimes globally.

To sum it all up if you'd like a real world example of moral hazard at work I'd invite you to look at what's going on in Greece right now. It's a country that has expanded entitlements so much that the cart is full and there's nobody left to pull it. It's hard to argue that anybody's situation in Greece has been improved, except perhaps that of the politicians.

To understand this principle, I'm going to allude to a rather famous hypothetical situation known as "The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas." Omelas is a utopia, but in order to maintain its utopian status a single child must be kept in perpetual misery through torture. Now I invite you to answer this question: is it ethical that only one innocent person be made to suffer if it guarantees the happiness of many others?

Your answer to this question determines if you are egoist, or utilitarian. An egoist (like libertarians) would say that it is absolutely unacceptable and unethical. My happiness and welfare should not be at the expense of another. A utilitarian would say the opposite. A utilitarian would state that since overall more people are happy than discontent, it is an ethically acceptable situation.

Just saying that something is or isn't unethical invites logical fallacy, because the entire definition of what is ethical is subjective. For myself and other libertarians, yes, it is unethical that the government wants to make some suffer in order to benefit another. A utilitarian would say that it's perfectly fine.

Perhaps I didn't explain well. The moral hazard was an idea that was first created by the economist John Maynard Keynes. Keynesian economics are the economic principle that all socialist democracies, and most "progressive" economic policies are based upon. Essentially it's "demand-side economics," while its counterpart is "supply-side economics." The idea is that if you give resources to the people, then they will spend the resources and fuel the economy. The counter-argument is to give resources to suppliers to drive down prices to make goods affordable and fuel the economy.

Keynes recognized the "moral hazard" of this type of economics, which is that once you give something to the people you can't take it back, and you create a situation that is eventually unsustainable. You have to continually give more and more to people every time the economy takes a dip, and eventually you'll reach a point where there is no incentive for people to work since the products of their labor are no longer their own. Keynes believed that in some situations it was worth it to do this, but even he knew the risks.

So to me the moral hazard is unethical because you are setting people up to fail. You are not giving them more tools to succeed, you are taking them away. You are reducing the incentive for people to work, and making them dependent on programs that cannot succeed in perpetuity. Eventually it will all collapse, and you are forcing a situation where the government must steal more and more (be it from its citizens, or perhaps from the citizens of another country) in order to sustain itself. Communism is the ultimate example of a moral hazard, and I one need hardly mention the atrocities of Stalin, Pol Pot, Mao, Kim Jong-Il, or any other communist leaders to point out why I consider it unethical and immoral.
